items.summary: Explains data contracts as API-style interface definitions for datasets, using the Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) YAML format to specify schema, semantics, quality rules, SLAs, and terms of use. Covers the defining properties of a contract (machine-readable, verifiable, versioned, provider-driven) and why explicit metadata matters for AI agents that consume data autonomously.
items.title: Data Contracts

items.summary: Describes Frostbite, a CPU architecture based on interaction nets, designed end-to-end by AI agent swarms from ISA through RTL to GDS, claiming 4.59x perf/W over an in-order superscalar core. Explains why interaction nets expose parallelism and locality, and how a formal spec language (ASL, lowered to Lean) served as the single source of truth with a fast system model calibrated against RTL power. Partly a company showcase, but contains real detail on agent-driven hardware design methodology.
items.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI

items.summary: Explains a Ruby heap buffer overflow in string case conversion for legacy single-byte encodings (German sharp s uppercasing to SS), and how Rack's MethodOverride middleware makes default Rails and Sinatra apps reachable before authentication. Also covers the affected versions, the limits of WAF mitigation such as origin bypass and non-HTTP entry points, and the steps to patch.
items.title: How Cloudflare WAF protects against ruby2shell (CVE-2026-132825)

items.summary: Podcast episode notes with CodeRabbit CEO Harjot Gill on running AI agent 'software factories', shipping thousands of PRs monthly at high AI spend. Covers verification layers for agents (TLA+/Lean, deterministic simulation, API emulation, staged rollouts with agent monitoring), replacing per-PR human review with release-level review and a strike-based review-exempt system, and hiring and cost tradeoffs.
items.title: Software factories and code reviews with Harjot Gill

items.summary: Explains five nginx memory-corruption vulnerabilities (HTTP/2 integer overflow, HTTP/3, resolver, mail proxy use-after-frees) plus a related Linux SCTP privilege-escalation bug, and why terminating HTTP/2/3 at a reverse proxy shields origins from protocol-level attacks. Covers where that protection stops, how to lock origins to the proxy, and concrete patching and mitigation steps.
items.title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them

items.summary: Describes how Bee built a zero-operator-access architecture on AWS using NitroTPM-based EC2 instance attestation, measured boot extended to containers and model weights via PCR14, and a public Sigstore Rekor transparency log. Clients release short-lived, in-memory-only encryption keys only to instances whose attestation, embedded in TLS certificates, checks out. The post also covers the controls attestation can't measure: network isolation, ephemeral storage, and separation of duties enforced with SCPs.
items.title: How Bee implemented Zero Operator Access for personal AI on AWS

items.summary: Netflix engineers describe the intelligence layer behind AI Discover, a TV app tab that offers steerable, theme-based recommendations with explanations and narrower follow-up themes. The post covers how they used generative AI while keeping latency, reliability and safety acceptable on TV devices. The excerpt is truncated, so the depth of the architectural details is not visible.
items.title: Engineering AI Discover

items.summary: A link-roundup from Martin Fowler covering an experiment showing healthier code reduces agent review costs by 22-35%, Steve Yegge on pacing AI software factories to human speed, and Chad Fowler's vision of SaaS as a slow-changing platform layer under customer-specific agent-built apps. Also includes off-topic items on Nvidia leadership, AI corrigibility, and Meta's agent suing Meta.
items.title: Fragments: November 20

items.summary: Walks through using AWS's Emulator (a local emulation of AWS API endpoints) to test Terraform applies before running against real infrastructure, catching errors that terraform plan misses. Covers provider configuration for redirecting endpoints, running the emulator in Docker locally, and a GitHub Actions workflow with signature checks and CA bundle setup.
items.title: Testing Terraform with AWS Emulator

items.summary: Describes how Cognition built per-session macOS VMs for its Devin coding agent on EC2 Mac Dedicated Hosts using Apple's Virtualization framework. Covers disk snapshotting via an NBD frontend to S3, a user-space Ethernet gateway for per-session network policy enforcement, pre-baked guest images that avoid permission dialogs, low-latency live video streaming, and use of the accessibility tree instead of screenshots for agent control.
items.title: AI coding agents on Amazon EC2 Mac: How Cognition scales Devin for macOS

items.summary: A talk transcript arguing that leaderless, quorum-based replication deserves more production use, built around a running example database called CashDB. It walks through ABD majority quorums, Megastore-style multi-Paxos, and EPaxos, and explains where each falls short on contention latency, local snapshots, and replica catch-up. It then evaluates newer work against those criteria: QuePaxa, Neo4j's RIOT DAG protocol, and Cassandra's Accord.
items.title: Please Implement A Quorum Database

items.summary: Rust 1.100 stabilizes the never type (with Infallible becoming an alias and a fallback change in older editions), the core Allocator trait for Vec and Box, DropGuard for scope-exit closures with rollback, and conjure_zst for unsafe ZST creation. On the Cargo side it adds unused-dependency warnings, a reorganized build-dir layout that reduces cache collisions, and min-publish-age dependency cooldowns as a supply-chain defense.
items.title: Rust 1.100

items.summary: A hands-on account of reverse-engineering a Wi-Fi air purifier to remove cloud dependency, covering setting up a transparent MitM proxy on a Raspberry Pi with nftables, intercepting TLS traffic, and discovering the device bootstraps its root CA over plain HTTP. Demonstrates practical IoT protocol analysis techniques including mitmproxy plugins and MQTT discovery.
items.title: Reverse engineering my Coway air purifier to ditch the cloud

items.summary: Argues that when AI agents write both production and test code, developers lose confidence in tests, and proposes treating developers as customers who own customer-level acceptance tests expressed as data in readable DSLs, interpreted by small test runners that are harder for agents to silently modify. It draws on XP acceptance tests, Fit, specification by example, Go table tests, and approval testing, and explains why mock-heavy AI-generated unit tests and prose specs fall short.
items.title: Tests as data: ensuring AI-generated code does what we want

items.summary: BurntSushi announces Jiff 1.0, a Rust datetime library, and walks through its API. The tour covers civil time, timestamps, time zones and offsets, and how Jiff resolves DST gaps and folds with configurable disambiguation strategies. It also explains why the API puts time zones front and center and why Jiff commits to long-term semver stability.
items.title: A datetime library for Rust

items.summary: Describes Superfluid, an open-source local LLM server that schedules interactive requests ahead of agent work, shares prompt prefix computation, and logs tokens durably on a single device. It also federates heterogeneous machines into one endpoint with speed-weighted load balancing and fault tolerance for nodes joining or failing. Evaluations show large first-token latency gains over llama-server and Ollama and scaling across multi-vendor fleets.
items.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference

items.summary: An interview with Sean Allen (Antithesis, Pony language) on software correctness: using strong ML-style type systems and exhaustive matching to make illegal states unrepresentable, why tests are a late-stage tool, property-based testing and workload-based verification like the Bank Test. It also covers quality as a design concern rather than a CI gate, tech debt, the difficulty of defending against supply chain attacks, and garbage collection design in Pony.
items.title: Software correctness & supply chain security, with Sean Allen

items.summary: Meta describes Intelligent Delivery, a system that decides where compute goes in its ads serving stack. It uses a shared request-understanding model (6B sparse parameters) that predicts the marginal utility of extra compute per request. A hierarchy of allocation engines covers region traffic shifting, matching hardware SKUs to workloads, and per-host constrained optimization under tail-latency SLOs, and AI agents propose and run tuning experiments.
items.title: Intelligent Delivery: Making Every Unit of Compute Serve Better Ads

items.summary: Netflix describes how it built an automated system to check the factual accuracy of show and episode synopses against source material, likely using LLM-based evaluation. The post covers making the checking both more accurate and cheaper to run at scale. The excerpt is truncated, so the depth of the technical detail is uncertain.
items.title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System

items.summary: Covers the security incident at cloud platform Railway, drawing on their detailed postmortem, including the attacker's likely use of 'abliterated' AI models without safeguards and how Railway hardened its systems afterward. The excerpt is truncated and part of a broader news roundup, so depth is uncertain.
items.title: The Pulse: What can we learn from the Railway hack?

items.summary: Explains a critical remote use-after-free in the Linux IPv4 TCP handshake: request-socket IP options were freed with kfree instead of kfree_rcu while other CPUs could still read them. Covers affected kernels and distro patch status, why Go's default MPTCP listeners matter, how to check hosts with ss -M, and an nftables mitigation that drops TCP packets carrying IPv4 options.
items.title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8

items.summary: Cloudflare explains how Privacy Pass and its successor MOLE (issuer-hiding endorsements and credentials) can move to post-quantum cryptography. It covers why token privacy already survives quantum attacks while unforgeability does not, and introduces VOLE-in-the-Head zero-knowledge proofs, MQ-based signatures like KuMQuat and UOV, and the tradeoffs in signature size and composability.
items.title: The post-quantum future of web privacy

items.summary: Dropbox describes the architecture behind its file-acting AI agent. The agent runs in per-conversation QEMU snapshot-restored VMs that come up in milliseconds and reach Dropbox files through rclone. Permission checks and credential injection sit in a host-side proxy outside the VM, and the piece also covers the Codex App Server JSON-RPC protocol (threads/turns/items), harness adapters, plan approval, and version-history rollback.
items.title: How two engineer side projects became the agent taking action inside Dropbox

items.summary: Describes building a Virtio-FS driver for Redox OS and porting it to boot on Cloud Hypervisor, including an explanation of how hardware virtualization, nested paging, and VirtIO devices work. Walks through concrete bugs encountered, such as legacy 8259 interrupt routing and a missing PIT/HPET timer that broke sleeps and preemption, fixed by using the local APIC TSC-deadline timer.
items.title: Virtualized Redox: from Virtio-FS to Cloud Hypervisor, and beyond

items.summary: Explains read, write, and space amplification as the gap between logical database requests and the physical storage work they trigger. Compares how B-trees and LSM trees trade off these amplifications, and covers how indexes, Bloom filters, compression, and caching affect them. The provided text is only the introduction and outline, so how deep the full article goes is unclear.
items.title: The Hidden Work Behind Every Database Request

items.summary: Podcast episode notes with Maude Lemaire covering scaling challenges at Slack and GitHub: thundering herds from emoji reactions in huge channels, event floods for power users, building the Koi Pond load-testing tool for 500k WebSocket connections, and how ActiveRecord-driven scatter queries capped GitHub at 16 shards. It also touches on using AI for foundational work and rotating platform and product engineers.
items.title: Scaling Slack and GitHub with Maude Lemaire

items.summary: Applies the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model to self-service platforms for data mesh and data products, using domain storytelling to contrast provisional, operational, scalable, and optimizing levels. It explains the 'platform gap' between data product/contract concepts and underlying tools like Spark, Iceberg, and S3, and why ticketing and IaC scripts alone still leave developers gluing components together.
items.title: The Data Product Platform Navigator

items.summary: Martin Fowler argues that LLM-drafted prose carries a recognizable 'voice' that puts readers off, and advises writers not to let LLMs draft or rephrase their work, though outlines may be acceptable. He frames writing as a tool for thinking, so delegating it to LLMs means delegating comprehension too. He also covers exceptions such as disability, translation, and form documents, and describes his site's AI-disclosure policy.
items.title: LLM Voice

items.summary: Meta describes F3 Lightning, which decouples per-feature releases of ads ML features from a single merged compute graph while keeping shared execution efficiency. It covers content-derived stable identifiers for deduplicating computation, building a single flattened execution plan at startup with failure isolation, a shared per-request memory buffer for cache locality, and dense index mapping to remove hash lookups. The result is ~3.6x faster time-to-production with no added compute cost.
items.title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale

items.summary: Cloudflare argues that remotely hosted AI agents act as intermediaries that strip websites of the identity, reputation, and accountability signals they use for fraud prevention, monetization, and compliance. It catalogs concrete problems such as friendly fraud, traffic commingling, broken risk-based auth, and account sharing. It also explains why human-in-the-loop CAPTCHAs and scoped permissions fail to solve them, and proposes the principle that the user–site relationship must survive intermediation.
items.title: Agents aren’t humans (but they kinda are)

items.summary: Pinterest engineers describe how they pre-train large ID embedding tables and fine-tune them inside the Homefeed ranking model. The focus is on making multi-epoch training safe, meaning it avoids the overfitting that is typical when ID embeddings see the same data repeatedly, while keeping the infrastructure efficient. The excerpt is truncated, so how deep the detail goes is uncertain.
items.title: Safe and Efficient Multi-Epoch Embedding Training

items.summary: The PHP Foundation explains how two critical RCE vulnerabilities in PHP's memory management and error handling were found, why the fix stalled for months over compatibility trade-offs, and how coordinated disclosure was disrupted by leaks and an embargo break. It also covers changes to security team processes and the growing role of AI tools in vulnerability discovery and triage.
items.title: Today's PHP security release, and how we're strengthening security

items.summary: Presents AutoParallel, a PyTorch-native planner that jointly searches parallelization strategies (data, tensor, pipeline, expert) for distributed training and emits ordinary PyTorch programs that compose with the compile stack and user-written distributed code. On dense, hybrid and MoE models across up to 128 H100s, it matches or beats expert TorchTitan recipes by up to 18.3% throughput and finds plans that hand-written recipes don't express.
items.title: AutoParallel: Composable, PyTorch-Native Automatic Parallelism for Production Training

items.summary: Cloudflare follows up on the eMudhra CA weak intermediate key incident, describing how they patched internal systems (including AI-assisted code analysis to find trust points), logged handshakes in Pingora to detect forged certificates, and measured client patching via probe connections from challenge pages. It shows that modern browsers are mostly patched but bots, embedded WebViews, and many networks still accept the compromised chain, and argues for dynamically updatable trust stores.
items.title: 4 real? Tracking exploitation and patching of eMudhra’s weak keys

items.summary: Meta announces open-weight release of Muse Spark Open, an 816B-parameter (42B active) MoE multimodal model with 1M context, aimed at coding and agentic tasks. It covers availability across inference engines and hosts, running it locally on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX using unified memory, and custom Helion kernels in SGLang. Technical depth is limited; it's mainly a release announcement.
items.title: Muse Spark Open

items.summary: Describes how Meta redesigned its Andromeda ads retrieval system by co-designing a mixture-of-experts retrieval model, fused GPU kernels, and a co-located single-GPU pipeline, reaching over a billion ads scored per second. It explains why retrieval at this scale is bound by memory bandwidth and network traffic, and how kernel fusion, moving index matching onto the GPU, and INT8 quantization address those limits.
items.title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design

items.summary: Rachel Laycock argues that experienced developers' hesitancy toward fully agentic coding stems from knowing that built software isn't the same as software that works in production. She describes a Thoughtworks experiment where a team built an app entirely with agents, spending most time on domain design and test/CI harnesses, yet struggled with a frequently red build, and she raises open questions about TDD, batch size, and CI/CD in the agentic era.
items.title: Why are good developers so wary of agentic development?

items.summary: Podcast summary with Titus Winters covering Google's large-scale C++ refactoring (AST parsing via MapReduce, coexisting APIs, sharded changes), why Google mandated tests, and the readability review program. It also discusses AI's mixed effect on outages and productivity, plus critiques of the CS curriculum and career advice for new engineers.
items.title: Software engineering at Google & CS education with Titus Winters

items.summary: Meta describes PrivacyLib, a shared library embedded in clients of hundreds of data systems that enforces and observes privacy requirements at the point of data access via pluggable enforcing and observing modules. It covers how they achieve coverage (typed clients plus RPC boundaries), scale (build-time compiled policies, in-process caching for billions of checks/sec), and reliability (per-service rollout), with a concrete code walkthrough of Policy Zones protecting messaging metadata and agent-context propagation for AI agents.
items.title: PrivacyLib: Privacy Controls at the Data Access Boundary

items.summary: Meta describes its production system for LLM-generated 'catching' tests that run against risky diffs before landing. The system uses intent-aware and mutation-based 'dodgy diff' generation workflows, then filters false positives with an LLM-as-judge ensemble plus a rule-based assessor, escalating to engineers only when warranted. Reported results include a 60% true-positive rate and 74 serious privacy bugs caught at the diff stage.
items.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale

items.summary: Karpathy argues that understanding of LLM capability is splitting into a funnel. Most people barely use LLMs, casual users see weak free-tier chatbots, professionals in math and code see large agentic productivity gains, and a few insiders work with far stronger systems. He attributes the gap to problem ambition, jagged capability that peaks in verifiable domains trained with RL, and access tier.
items.title: The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening

items.summary: Netflix describes how Pensive, its system for auto-diagnosing and remediating failed data workloads across Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid, moved from regex and hand-written Java rules to an AI-assisted approach. The piece covers the scale involved (around 100k failures on peak days), how errors are classified into user versus platform causes, and how the system produces retry or remediation guidance reliably.
items.title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI

items.summary: Netflix describes an automated system that reframes horizontal video into vertical and other aspect ratios for its in-app Clips feed and social marketing, replacing manual editor reframing. The post covers how cropping decisions are made and how the system plugs into internal production tooling at scale.
items.title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing

items.title: Clef: Open-weight decision models, and new RL fine-tuning platform

items.summary:
Aleph Alpha Kolibri: How the Sovereign German LLM Works
Kolibri is an open-weight large language model (LLM) from Aleph Alpha for German and English: a mixture of experts with 78 billion parameters that only uses about 3.5 billion of them for each token it reads or writes. It…
items.title: Aleph Alpha Kolibri: How the sovereign German LLM works

items.summary: Cloudflare explains how it replaced fixed, per-zone range-size caching (nginx-style slicing) with a Pingora-based design that aligns origin fetches to on-disk cache chunks and composes responses from cached, in-flight, and newly fetched bytes. It covers validation rules (ETag, size, If-Range, compression) for correct 206 responses and reports production results for R2: roughly halved p99 TTFB and about 6% less tiered cache traffic.
items.title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning

items.summary: Cloudflare describes how its GeoKey Manager restricts where customer private keys can be unwrapped, replacing attribute-based encryption with regional symmetric root keys that derive hybrid ML-KEM-768/X25519 HPKE key pairs. It covers the key hierarchy (service context, region, epoch) and how blast radius is scoped across it. It also explains TPM-backed provisioning of root keys to edge servers, storage in the kernel keyring, and fail-closed behavior when a key is missing.
items.title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management

items.summary: We are changing turbopuffer's storage architecture to take search to the next level. turbopuffer v3 changes how documents and indexes are laid out, written, compacted, and queried in turbopuffer. It will allow us to make search faster in every respect — including text, regex,…
items.title: RIP, vector database

items.summary: Netflix's Java Platform team describes Quasar, a tool that maps proposed API changes in shared libraries to actual symbol references across many consumer repositories. It explains how this blast-radius evidence informs release decisions such as removing deprecated APIs, and how it can give coding agents cross-repo context for migrations.
items.title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes

items.summary: Describes OpenLDK, a JIT compiler and runtime that translates JVM bytecode into Common Lisp so SBCL compiles it to native code, with Java classes mapped to CLOS classes and lazy per-method compilation with a persistent code cache. It shows polyglot interop across Kotlin, Scala, Clojure, Groovy and others, CLOS method combination around Java methods, exception/condition mapping, and saving a warmed Spring Boot app in a Lisp image for fast startup.
items.title: OpenLDK: Bringing the Java World into Common Lisp

items.summary:
Big Tech ruined the cloud, so we’re renaming ours
From ever-increasing subscription prices to outages and data harvesting: we don’t like what the cloud has come to represent. So we’re redefining what an online service should be: private, optional, and free from lock-in or walled…
items.title: Big Tech ruined the cloud, so we're renaming ours

items.summary: Netflix describes how its Kubernetes-based Titus container platform, which is multi-tenant by default, added a single-tenant mode that gives certain workloads VM-level isolation. The piece covers why some workloads don't fit shared hosts and how the platform supports dedicated instances while keeping the same container experience for application teams.
items.title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform

items.summary: GitHub explains how it migrated nearly all Git repositories to Azure and why the busiest ones were blocked by cross-region write latency under a repository-wide quorum lock. It describes moving to per-reference quorum serialization (3-4x write throughput) and adding object storage as a 'virtual replica' so stateless read replicas can scale independently from writes.
items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure

items.summary: Arthur O'Dwyer discusses how compiler warnings should handle fixits, specifically the tension between offering a fix that changes behavior to match likely intent and one that silences the warning while keeping current behavior, with Clang and GCC examples. He also argues that suppression mechanisms such as extra parentheses work like error-correcting codes and signaling. Under that view, warnings should compare how much "ornamentation" the code has relative to its typo-corrected version, rather than follow absolute rules.
items.title: Two musings on the design of compiler warnings (2020)

items.summary: Netflix describes how it built an ontology-backed knowledge graph that connects services, telemetry, and dependencies across its infrastructure, so engineers can trace regressions end to end. The post covers why dashboards and team-scoped views break down at billions of requests and tens of millions of log events per second, and how a shared semantic model cuts the time to find a root cause.
items.title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale

items.summary: Presents KVStream, a KV cache engine for long-context LLM serving that treats prefix retrieval as aggregate-bandwidth scheduling across storage tiers (node-local NVMe plus the parallel or cloud file system). It batches a step's reads, defers writes behind the forward pass, replicates chunks on every tier, and has each tier pull the next unread chunks once it is free. A performance model shows why this beats static splits, and the evaluation on up to 128 GPUs reports up to 1.49x throughput and 6.1x lower TTFT compared with LMCache.
items.title: KVStream: Adaptive Parallel Storage Management for KV Caching in Large-Scale LLM Serving

items.summary: An empirical study of 335 real failures across 40 open-source LLM GUI-agent applications, where the tools that capture screenshots or UI trees and execute actions leave the agent's view out of sync with the live interface. The failures fall into 11 defect patterns covering state representation, state transition, and synchronization, and most of them are silent. The authors also present MalvaGuard, a static contract checker that reaches 57.3% precision and 76.8% recall on a separate 20-application corpus.
items.title: Understanding Tool-Mediated Interaction Failures in Agentic GUI Software: An Empirical Study

items.summary: An experience report from modernizing a fleet of about 800,000 battery-powered retail IoT sensors across 3000 stores. It shows how familiar practices change shape under physical constraints: hardware-in-the-loop development with sensor farms, firmware-level self-diagnostics, and virtual device emulators for scale testing. It also covers designing for intermittent connectivity, treating energy as a design concern, and OTA updates with resumable state, partition swapping and staged rollouts.
items.title: When Software Meets Hardware

items.summary: Netflix describes how it integrates a centralized transformer-based foundation model for member preference learning into downstream personalization applications. It covers practical integration patterns such as distributing learned embeddings and representations to specialized models, along with the trade-offs involved in serving and adoption.
items.title: Integrating Netflix’s Foundation Model into Personalization applications

items.summary: Meta describes building its Forum app with agents running plan-implement-test loops under engineer supervision, gated by automated verification (builds, tests, UI spec matching, navigation agents). It covers operating-model pieces (rules, skills, commands, hooks), giving agents tools to inspect live state, sandbox build flavors that compile prototype code out of production, and agent-driven stress testing that found a memory issue.
items.title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering

items.summary: Podcast episode notes with Uber Distinguished Engineer Uday Kiran Medisetty on how Uber's decade of developer infrastructure (DevPods, M3DB, Cadence, Jaeger, service registries) underpins its AI agent tooling. Covers the Model Gateway for vendor-agnostic LLM access, harness abstraction, token spend controls, AI-assisted code review with risk scores, CI overload mitigation, and measuring productivity by PR type.
items.title: Uber’s AI infra, from the inside

items.summary: GitHub explains how it replaced stargazer-list scraping with an aggregate star history endpoint. The post covers why the old endpoint was expensive, including a pagination bug that counted all stars on every request. It also explains why aggregating before OFFSET/LIMIT doesn't reduce database work, and how filtering by an indexed time range before grouping cut requests for large repos from about 2,500 to 24 while removing identity exposure.
items.title: From 2,500 requests to 24: Rebuilding star history without the stargazers

items.summary: GitHub describes Evergreen, a Go-based GitHub App that automates quarterly outside-collaborator access reviews and stale repo archival using scheduled Actions, webhooks, issue-ops, custom properties, and git-committed JSON state as an audit trail. It covers fail-secure/fail-closed design, partial-failure handling, dry-run rollout, observability, and pacing around secondary rate limits.
items.title: Staying Evergreen: How we automated secure access and repo hygiene in a shared org

items.summary: Airbnb describes CASTLE, an approach to bootstrapping a natural language search ranking model before any real user queries exist by jointly generating synthetic queries and relevance labels from de-identified booking and search signals. Readers learn how the team framed the cold-start problem and used synthetic data generation to train retrieval and ranking for NL search.
items.title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query

items.summary: Meta describes how its infrastructure handled record World Cup 2026 traffic, including WhatsApp peaks of 30M messages/sec, and the finding that traffic surged during match breaks rather than gameplay. It covers pre-provisioned capacity buffers, country-level graceful degradation, cascade prevention, per-region peak forecasting when all regions spike simultaneously, and the decision not to freeze deployments.
items.title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale

items.summary: Airbnb describes a system that captures real production MySQL-compatible database traffic and replays it offline. They use it for load testing, capacity planning, de-risking version upgrades and migrations, and reproducing incidents across hundreds of clusters handling millions of QPS.
items.title: Beyond synthetic testing: Capturing and replaying real database workloads at Airbnb

items.summary: Meta explains its deployment of Network Time Security (RFC 8915) on its public time service, covering the NTS-KE handshake, authenticated NTP extension fields, and a stateless cookie design in which sealing keys are derived via HKDF from a master secret and the epoch day number instead of being replicated. It also covers why authenticated time matters as certificate lifetimes shrink, practical chrony configuration with pool, and the threats NTS does not address, such as delay attacks, bootstrapping, and servers that are authenticated but wrong.
items.title: NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta

items.summary: Podcast summary with Sam Newman covering microservices as an architecture of last resort, his three simplified rules of distributed systems, idempotency keys versus fingerprints, fail-open/fail-closed decisions, and Woods' four resilience concepts. It also discusses modular architecture as a way to constrain AI-assisted development, hedging LLM vendors, and recommended architecture reading.
items.title: Building resilient systems with Sam Newman

items.summary: Gergely Orosz summarizes his LDX3 keynote on how AI coding agents have reshaped software engineering: engineers running 5-10 parallel agents, agent-authored PRs overtaking human ones on GitHub, the decline of the IDE, and companies building internal agent harnesses. It also covers what's broken (code review, quality) and what remains unchanged, with data from GitHub, Linear, and Factory AI.
items.title: The state of the tech industry in 2026

items.summary: Explains LLM sycophancy: why models abandon correct answers under user pushback, tracing it to pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and RLHF reward models that conflate human approval with accuracy. Covers multi-turn pressure, social sycophancy, agreement masquerading as verification, and approaches like probes and pressure-resistance testing.
items.title: Why LLMs Agree With You Even When You’re Wrong

items.summary: Pinterest engineers describe how they use LLMs to turn raw user activity (clicks, saves, sessions over weeks) into higher-level 'journeys' representing user goals and intent. The piece covers the motivation for intent-level personalization and the system for generating journeys at scale. The excerpt is truncated, so the depth of the architecture discussion can't be fully confirmed.
items.title: From Activity to Intent: Generating User Journeys with LLMs

items.summary: Covers a trend at mid-sized tech companies like Ramp and Stripe of building internal AI 'vibe-coding' platforms that let non-engineers create internal websites and tools. The excerpt is truncated, so the depth of technical detail is unclear, but it gives a sense of how companies are adopting AI-assisted development internally.
items.title: The Pulse: new trend of building “internal vibe-coding apps” at tech companies

items.summary: Walks through designing an AI-assisted customer support reply workflow where the model only proposes drafts and the application enforces authorization, revision-bound human approval, and dispatch through an explicit state machine. Covers prompt injection boundaries, handling timeouts with a delivery_unknown state and reconciliation instead of blind retries, negative test cases, and what to log for auditability.
items.title: The AI Drafted a Reply. Who Authorized Sending It?

items.summary: Examines tenant isolation in multi-tenant SaaS across identity, data, compute, network, storage, performance, and operations, distinguishing authentication, authorization, and isolation. Covers shared vs dedicated vs hybrid models, trustworthy tenant context propagation, composite foreign keys for tenant ownership in PostgreSQL, and row-level security caveats.
items.title: Tenant Isolation and Resource Separation: Engineering Trust in Multi-Tenant Systems

items.summary: Explores why netip.AddrFrom16(ip.As16()) is about 8x slower than a native IPv4-to-IPv6 mapping method in Go, comparing stdlib, helper, and unsafe implementations with benchmarks and generated assembly. It then walks through the Go compiler's phases and IR dumps to patch the noder and optimize the pack/copy/unpack pattern.
items.title: Hacking the Go compiler to efficiently map IPv4 to IPv6

items.summary: A collection of short notes from Martin Fowler. The main thread argues that higher-level code still matters when LLMs write software, drawing on Sam Ruby's example that a Rails app of about 60K tokens grows to about 4M tokens in C, and on Unmesh Joshi's view of code as a conceptual model. Other notes cover the move from deterministic building to 'nurturing' inferential systems, an Evans/Fowler interview on AI, and hallucination-rate trade-offs between models.
items.title: Fragments: October 4

items.summary: Analyzes 150 production incidents in compound AI systems (RAG, tool-using, orchestrated LLM pipelines) to build a taxonomy of 23 failure modes across retrieval, generation, tool, orchestration, and integration categories. It proposes resilience patterns such as circuit breakers, output quality gates, and component isolation, and measures their effectiveness with fault injection experiments. Only the abstract is shown here, so the depth of the full paper is unverified.
items.title: Compound AI System Reliability: A Failure Taxonomy and Resilience Pattern Catalog from 150 Production Incidents

items.summary: A postmortem of a data pipeline bug where a non-unique cache key silently dropped 99.9% of records while jobs reported success. The author draws out three habits: row-conservation accounting with ratio floors at every stage boundary, idempotent reruns via deterministic natural keys, upserts and database unique constraints, and SCD Type 2 dimensions that use null-safe change detection.
items.title: A cache key ate 99.9% of my records and the pipeline looked green

items.summary: Walks through the four-phase zero-downtime migration playbook (dual-write, backfill, verify, cut over) with Python code for a phase-aware router, keyset-cursor backfill, and continuous sampling verification. Explains specific failure modes: backfilling before dual-write, stale backfill overwriting fresh writes, shadow-write failures coupling availability, and noisy verification. It also covers the harder edge cases: cross-store transactions, schema changes mid-migration, and non-key-value reads.
items.title: Zero-Downtime Database Migration: The Dual-Write Window Is Where It Goes Wrong

items.summary: Models an online feature store as a materialized view over an event stream and defines a per-feature freshness budget, proving a staleness bound and a closed-form threshold below which a feature can never be served in budget. Validates this in simulation and on a Kafka/Redis/PostgreSQL pipeline, and shows that phase-locked request and recomputation clocks in simulations systematically under-observe staleness.
items.title: Feature Freshness Budgets for Real-Time ML Inference Under Stream Lag

items.summary: Presents LOGOS, an unsupervised system that uses entity-event co-occurrence and temporal precedence to compress millions of raw, unannotated log lines into a compact precedence forest that shows how a failure propagated. It is evaluated on 25 enterprise outages and 12 open-source issues, where it removes about 99.8% of noise and consolidates alert floods 124x. Feeding its output to an LLM gave 80% (enterprise) and 100% (open-source) zero-shot root-cause accuracy.
items.title: From Alert Floods to Precedence Forests: Zero-Prior-Knowledge Incident Triage with LOGOS

items.summary: Presents Beaver, a system for co-locating latency-critical vRAN processing with best-effort ML workloads on a shared GPU. It resizes SM partitions at slot granularity based on scheduled work, and rewrites ML kernels so they yield HBM bandwidth during the vRAN's memory-critical phases. On an H200 it keeps p99.9 latency within a 1.5ms deadline while retaining 74% of Llama-3.3-70B serving throughput.
items.title: Beaver: Elastic GPU Sharing between ML and Latency-Critical vRAN Workloads
